candidates.attacker_control: Every element of `context.getRequestParameters()` (servlet `request.getParameterMap()`, i.e. POST form fields or query parameters) is attacker-controlled, including both the parameter name and the first value (`values[0]`) that is written unescaped. The attacker does not need an account or credentials; they only need the victim to submit a crafted POST to a pac4j-protected URL (e.g. an auto-submitting cross-site HTML form).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified the sink is real (no escaping applied to `values[0]`, and `escapeHtml` only escapes `&`, `<`, `"`, which is sufficient for a double-quoted attribute but is simply not applied). Verified the generated page is served as a response body (not as a redirect), so injected markup executes. Confirmed the sibling fields (parameter name, form action) ARE escaped, showing escaping was intended in this code path. Confirmed the saved content is only replayable in the victim's own session (attacker cannot simply fetch it), so a victim interaction (cross-site POST + login) is required, and confirmed no CSRF authorizer check blocks the initial POST because authorization checks occur only after authentication. Also checked comparable project hardening (SAML POST encoder uses `HTMLEncoder.encodeForHTMLAttribute` for form attributes) to confirm the project's intended pattern is to escape HTML form attributes. Cannot verify whether this line differs from the published upstream release or whether it corresponds to a known CVE/fix; it is reported as a source-level vulnerability in this snapshot, not a confirmed exploit.
candidates.impact: Reflected/stored cross-site scripting in the application's origin after login. Script can act as the authenticated victim: read non-HttpOnly state, invoke same-origin authenticated endpoints (including CSRF-token-protected APIs because script runs in-origin), and exfiltrate data. It also enables convincing phishing within the trusted origin. Severity depends on app content/session handling, but the sink is directly reachable from an attacker-controlled parameter.
candidates.prerequisites: Web application using the pac4j security filter with at least one indirect client (so `DefaultSecurityLogic.startAuthentication` is true and `DefaultSavedRequestHandler.save` runs) and the victim having no profile/session at POST time. The request must not be classified as AJAX by the configured `AjaxRequestResolver` (a plain cross-site form POST is not AJAX by default). Victim must complete authentication at the IdP/login form so the saved content is replayed by the callback logic.
candidates.root_cause: In `HttpActionHelper.buildFormPostContent` the parameter value is appended raw into a double-quoted hidden-input attribute: line 86 concatenates `... value=" + values[0] + " />`, whereas the same statement HTML-escapes the parameter name (`escapeHtml(entry.getKey())`) and line 81 escapes the form action URL (`escapeHtml(requestedUrl)`). `escapeHtml` (lines 98-100) escapes `&`, `<`, `"`, so the omission for `values[0]` removes the only neutralization on an attacker-controlled string.
candidates.title: Unescaped request parameter value in HttpActionHelper.buildFormPostContent allows XSS after login
candidates.trace: 1) Unauthenticated (or not-yet-profiled) victim POSTs attacker-chosen parameters to a matched protected URL. 2) `DefaultSecurityLogic.perform` (lines 90-153) finds no profiles and calls `saveRequestedUrl` (line 148) because the first current client is indirect. 3) `DefaultSavedRequestHandler.save` (line 25) sees `WebContextHelper.isPost(context)` true and calls `HttpActionHelper.buildFormPostContent(context)` (line 27), storing the generated HTML as an `OkAction` in the session under `pac4jRequestedUrl` (line 28). 4) The payload string is embedded verbatim at `HttpActionHelper` line 86 (`" value=\"" + values[0] + "\" />`); a value such as `"><script>...</script>` closes the attribute/tag and injects script. 5) After successful authentication, `DefaultCallbackLogic.redirectToOriginallyRequestedUrl` -> `DefaultSavedRequestHandler.restore` (lines 40-61) returns the stored `OkAction` content via `buildFormPostContentAction`. 6) The JEE adapter writes that HTML to the response body with HTTP 200 (`JEEHttpActionAdapter` lines 43-54), so the injected script executes in the application origin with the victim's newly established session.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-tested and not compared against upstream tags or patches. Whether the default matcher set/AJAX resolver in a particular application is configured such that a cross-site POST reaches `buildFormPostContent` was reasoned from source, not exercised. The exact CSP/header policy of a consuming application could mitigate execution but is outside this snapshot (pac4j's default security headers do not include a CSP).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

coverage_summary: Read a large share of the visible main sources: pac4j-core engine (DefaultSecurityLogic, DefaultCallbackLogic, DefaultLogoutLogic, exception handling), matching/authorization (matchers, CSRF generator/authorizer, default/custom authorizers, authorization generators, client finders, Clients/Config), profile handling (ProfileManager, ProfileDefinition, BasicUserProfile/CommonProfile, serializers), client base classes and callback/URL resolvers, cookie/session/JEE context and adapters, pac4j-jee, pac4j-http clients, pac4j-cas (client/config/redirect/proxy receptor/rest), pac4j-saml (client, config sampled, SSO authn response validator, logout validator, message receiver, signature trust engine, XML parser configuration, transports, metadata/keystore), pac4j-oidc (client, configuration, token validator, profile creator, redirection/logout), pac4j-jwt (generator, signature/encryption configurations, JWK helper), pac4j-oauth (redirect builders, profile creators, config builders), pac4j-sql/ldap/mongo profile services, pac4j-config builders, and documentation. Not every file was read end-to-end; files under hidden `credentials` paths could only be inferred from call sites.
limitations: 53 repository files were filtered out as sensitive by the harness and are not visible; these include the whole `org/pac4j/**/credentials/**` trees (Credentials types, `JwtAuthenticator`, `OidcExtractor`/`OidcAuthenticator` state check, BasicAuth/Digest/X509/Kerberos extractors and authenticators, password encoders). Those are exactly the places where an authentication bypass could hide, so this review cannot rule them out.

No test files are present in the snapshot, and no build, dependency resolution, or runtime execution/scanner was performed (and is not permitted), so reachability/impact statements are source-reasoned, not runtime-confirmed.

No network access and no comparison against upstream pac4j releases, patches, advisories or CVE data was allowed; therefore I could not determine whether the submitted code differs from the published upstream 5.2.0 sources or maps to a known CVE.
Only the single strongest candidate is reported per the review cap; several plausible but weaker/unconfirmed leads are listed above rather than as additional candidates.

rejected_leads.lead: CsrfAuthorizer.hashEquals compares String.hashCode() values instead of constant-time content equality (pac4j-core/.../authorization/authorizer/CsrfAuthorizer.java lines 61-85).
rejected_leads.reason: Weak comparison, but not shown practically exploitable: the attacker does not know the victim's 32-char random CSRF token, so passing the check requires guessing a 32-bit hash collision (about 2^-32 per request) against a per-request regenerated token. The surrounding comment documents the deliberate use of 'hash equalities', so this looks like an upstream design weakness/hardening opportunity rather than a concrete bypass. The empty-string edge case (previous token absent -> empty string) is real but applies to the first matched request of a session, when the victim has no authenticated profile to abuse.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultLogoutLogic matches the user-supplied `url` parameter with the default pattern `/.*`, which also matches protocol-relative URLs such as `//evil.com` or `/\evil.com`, producing an open redirect in `FoundAction` (DefaultLogoutLogic.java lines 74-85; Pac4jConstants.java line 59).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible open redirect, but the pattern and constant comment ('only relative urls are allowed by default') appear to be the upstream default; `logoutUrlPattern` is explicitly user-configurable and documented as the control point. No evidence in this snapshot that `//evil.com` was intended to be rejected, so it is reported as an unconfirmed lead, not the strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SAML2LogoutValidator accepts unsigned IdP logout requests: `validateLogoutRequest` only calls `validateSignatureIfItExists` (SAML2LogoutValidator.java line 120) and the IssueInstant check is intentionally commented out (lines 122-123), then destroys the session keyed by the request's NameID/sessionIndex (lines 143-152).
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker could potentially force victim logout (availability/CSRF-logout) with a forged request, but no signature-required policy is documented in this snapshot and the 'don't check because of CAS v5' comment shows intentional leniency; impact is session termination rather than account compromise. Not selected as top candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: ProfileDefinition.getParameter uses `parameters.length >= num` instead of `> num` (pac4j-core/.../profile/definition/ProfileDefinition.java lines 72-78), which can throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when length == num.
rejected_leads.reason: Off-by-one DoS only; reachable mainly through the JWT typed-id restore path (restoreProfileFromTypedId enabled only for JwtProfileDefinition) with an empty parameter array, and the JWT authenticator/credential classes that would invoke it are hidden from this snapshot. Impact and reachability are too weak/uncertain to submit.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultAjaxRequestResolver.buildAjaxResponse escapes only '&' when embedding the redirection URL into the `<redirect url="...">` partial-response XML (pac4j-core/.../http/ajax/DefaultAjaxRequestResolver.java lines 51-59).
rejected_leads.reason: The URL originates from server-side redirection builders (provider metadata/config), not directly from request parameters, so attacker control is not established. Reported as a lead only.

summary: Reviewed the pac4j 5.2.0-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (640 of 693 files visible) as a defensive source review. Traced the core authentication/authorization engine, CSRF matcher/authorizer, saved-request handling, profile management, SAML/OIDC/JWT/CAS/HTTP clients, and the JEE adapters. One candidate is submitted: an HTML-injection/XSS in the form-post page built by `HttpActionHelper.buildFormPostContent`, where request-parameter values are concatenated into an `<input value=\"...\">` attribute without HTML escaping while the sibling parameter name and the form action are escaped. Other plausible issues are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads. No runtime or patch/ground-truth confirmation was performed; all findings are source-level leads.
